title: Excel Automation with Macros & VBA
tagline: Record, read, write and debug macros, with code you can run in your own Excel
summary: Automate Excel the way professionals do. Decide what is worth automating, record and read macros, write VBA with variables, decisions and loops, work with ranges and sheets, handle errors, debug step by step and design macros others can trust. VBA runs inside desktop Excel, so every lesson gives code you can run in your own copy, and the practice labs train the thinking: choosing what to automate, predicting code, spotting errors and checking a macro's result with formulas.

modules.title: Macros: first steps
modules.summary: Understand what a macro and VBA are, record and run a macro, save a macro-enabled file, and handle macro security with care.
modules.outcome: You can decide whether a task is worth automating, record a simple macro, run it safely and read what it recorded.
modules.intro: If you do the same thing in Excel every week (format a report, clean an export, copy data between files), a macro can do it for you in one click. A macro is a recorded or written list of instructions that Excel follows. They are written in VBA (Visual Basic for Applications), the programming language built into Excel and the other Office programs. You do not need to be a programmer to start: Excel can record your actions and write the first code for you.

topics.title: What a macro is and when to use one
topics.html:
A macro is a saved set of instructions. VBA is the language those instructions are written in. When you press a button or a shortcut, Excel carries the instructions out faster, and the same way, every time.

Good and poor candidates for a macro
Good for a macroPoor fit
Repeated every day, week or monthDone once
Follows fixed rulesNeeds human judgement each time
Identical structure each timeThe layout changes constantly
Many rows or many filesA handful of cells
Boring and error-prone by handQuicker to do than to automate
Worked example

The Monday report

Every Monday you spend twenty minutes formatting the same report.

  1. Twenty minutes a week is about seventeen hours a year.
  2. A macro that does it in one click might take two hours to build and test.
  3. It pays for itself in about six weeks, and removes the typing mistakes.

Answer. Automate when the time saved over a year clearly beats the time to build, test and maintain.

Watch out

A macro is a program that can change or delete data across a whole workbook in a second. Test on a copy, and keep a backup of anything important before running a new macro.

Try it yourself: You must write a personal reply to each customer complaint. Is that a macro job?

Model answer. No. Each reply needs judgement and the right tone, which a fixed set of rules cannot provide.

Check what you just learned

1. Which task suits a macro?
  • Deciding who gets a discount case by case
  • Formatting the same weekly report (correct)
  • A one-off clean-up
  • Writing thoughtful replies

It is repeated, rule-based and identical.

2. What is VBA?
  • A kind of chart
  • A file type
  • The language macros are written in (correct)
  • A spreadsheet function

Visual Basic for Applications is the language behind macros.
keyPoints: A macro is a saved set of instructions written in VBA.
Automate work that is repeated, rule-based and identical each time.
Test macros on a copy and keep a backup.

topics.title: Record and run your first macro
topics.html:
The macro recorder watches what you do and writes the VBA for you. It is the best way to learn: you can do a task, then read the code it produced.

Running and managing macros
You want toDo this
See your macrosDeveloper > Macros, or press Alt+F8
Run a macroSelect it and click Run, or use its shortcut key
Open the code editorPress Alt+F11 (the Visual Basic Editor)
Run from a buttonInsert a shape or button and Assign Macro
Keep the macro in the fileSave as Excel Macro-Enabled Workbook (.xlsm)
Worked example

Record a header format

You always make the heading row bold and shaded.

  1. Click Record Macro, name it FormatHeader, then select A1:D1.
  2. Press Bold and choose a fill colour, then stop recording.
  3. Press Alt+F8, select FormatHeader and run it on another sheet.

Answer. One click now does what took four.

Watch out

An ordinary .xlsx file cannot store macros. If you save a workbook with macros as .xlsx, Excel warns you and the macros are lost. Use .xlsm.

Tip

Give recorded macros clear names such as FormatHeader or CleanExport, not Macro1. In a year you will thank yourself.

Check what you just learned

1. Which file type keeps macros?
  • .xlsx
  • .txt
  • .csv
  • .xlsm (correct)

.xlsm is the macro-enabled workbook.

2. How do you open the Visual Basic Editor?
  • Alt+F11 (correct)
  • Ctrl+Z
  • Alt+Tab
  • F5 only

Alt+F11 opens the editor.
keyPoints: The recorder writes VBA for the steps you perform.
Alt+F8 lists macros; Alt+F11 opens the code editor.
Macros are kept only in .xlsm files.

topics.title: Reading recorded code, and absolute versus relative recording
topics.html:
Open the editor and look at what the recorder wrote. You will see a Sub (a named block of instructions) containing lines that do one thing each. Each line is a sentence: an object, what to do with it, and sometimes a value.

Reading a line of recorded code
LineIn plain words
Range("A1:D1").SelectSelect the cells A1 to D1
Selection.Font.Bold = TrueMake the selected cells' font bold
Selection.Interior.Color = RGB(255, 242, 204)Fill the selected cells with a pale yellow
Sub FormatHeader() ... End SubA named macro that begins and ends here
Definition

Absolute and relative recording. By default the recorder is absolute: it records exact cell addresses such as A1:D1. With Use Relative References switched on it records movements relative to the active cell, so the macro works from wherever you start.

Worked example

Why the choice matters

You record a macro that formats the cell you click and the cell below it.

  1. Absolute: it always formats the same two cells, whatever you click first.
  2. Relative: it formats the cell you click and the one below, wherever you are.

Answer. Choose relative when the macro should work on whatever cell is active.

What recorded code does badly

  • It selects everything before acting on it, which is slow; good code works on a range directly.
  • It records every step, including ones you did by mistake.
  • It cannot decide or repeat: no If, no loops. You add those by writing code.

Common mistakes

  • Recording while you click around, so the macro contains useless steps.
  • Leaving the macro named Macro1.
  • Never opening the code to read it.

Check what you just learned

1. What does Selection.Font.Bold = True do?
  • Selects the cell
  • Makes the selected cells bold (correct)
  • Deletes the cells
  • Saves the file

It sets the bold property of the selection to True.

2. Recording with relative references means the macro:
  • Always uses A1
  • Cannot be run
  • Acts relative to the active cell (correct)
  • Runs on a timer

It follows where you start.
keyPoints: A Sub is a named macro; each line is an instruction.
Absolute recording uses fixed addresses; relative follows the active cell.
Recorded code selects too much and cannot decide or repeat.

topics.title: Macro security
topics.html:
A macro can do anything you can do in Excel, and more: open files, send data, delete things. That power is why attackers send macro-enabled files by email and ask you to click Enable Content.

Safe habits with macros
SafeRisky
Leave macros disabled for files from people you do not knowClick Enable Content on a file that arrived unexpectedly
Read the code of a macro you were given before running itRun any macro you find online without reading it
Keep macros in files you wrote, saved as .xlsmTurn macro security down to Enable all macros
Keep a backup before running a new macroRun a new macro on your only copy
Watch out

Never lower the macro security setting to Enable all macros. It turns off the one protection that stops a harmful macro running automatically.

Things to be suspicious of in a macro

  • Code that downloads something from the internet.
  • Code that works with files and folders you did not expect it to touch.
  • Code that hides itself or tries to confuse the reader.
  • A document that says the content is 'protected' and you must enable macros to see it.
Tip

Excel's default asks before running macros in files from the internet. Keep that default.

Check what you just learned

1. A file arrives unexpectedly and asks you to Enable Content. You should:
  • Click Enable at once
  • Lower macro security
  • Forward it
  • Not enable it, and check with the sender another way (correct)

Unexpected macro files are a common way to spread malware.

2. What is the safest macro security setting to keep?
  • Disable with notification (ask first) (correct)
  • Enable all macros
  • Delete Excel
  • Never save files

Asking first keeps you in control.

Key terms: flip and sort

Macro
A saved set of instructions
VBA
The language macros are written in
Sub
A named block of VBA code
Macro recorder
Writes code from your actions
.xlsm
The file type that keeps macros
Enable Content
The button that lets a file's macros run
keyPoints: Macros can do harm, so enable them only for files you trust.
Never set macro security to Enable all.
Read unknown code, and keep backups before running new macros.

modules.title: VBA building blocks
modules.summary: Write your first VBA: the editor, Subs, variables and data types, operators, message and input boxes, and clear comments.
modules.outcome: You can write a short, readable Sub that asks for input, calculates and reports a result.
modules.intro: VBA reads like a very strict version of English. A line says do this to that. In this module you learn the grammar: where code lives, how to store values in variables, the kinds of value there are, and how to talk to the user. These few ideas appear in every macro you will ever write.

topics.title: The editor and your first Sub
topics.html:
Press Alt+F11 to open the Visual Basic Editor. On the left is the Project Explorer, listing your workbook and its modules; the big window on the right is where code is written. Code lives in a module (Insert > Module).

The editor at a glance
PartUse it for
Project ExplorerBrowse workbooks, sheets and modules
Code windowWrite and edit code
Immediate window (Ctrl+G)Try a line at once and see Debug.Print output
Properties windowChange names and settings of objects

The anatomy of a Sub

  • It starts with Sub and a name, with brackets.
  • It ends with End Sub.
  • Lines in between are the instructions, one per line, indented for readability.
  • A line beginning with an apostrophe ' is a comment, a note for humans.
Tip

Put your cursor anywhere inside a Sub and press F5 to run it. Press F8 to step through it one line at a time.

Common mistakes

  • Writing code outside any Sub.
  • Spaces in the name of a Sub: use HelloGrowQR or Hello_GrowQR.
  • Forgetting End Sub.
  • Forgetting the quotation marks around text.

Check what you just learned

1. Which line ends a macro?
  • Stop
  • End Sub (correct)
  • Close
  • Exit

A Sub always ends with End Sub.

2. What does an apostrophe at the start of a line do?
  • Runs the line twice
  • Stops the macro
  • Makes it a comment that VBA ignores (correct)
  • Prints it

It marks a note for humans.
keyPoints: Alt+F11 opens the editor; code lives in modules.
A Sub runs from Sub to End Sub.
F5 runs, F8 steps, an apostrophe starts a comment.

topics.title: Variables and data types
topics.html:
A variable is a named box that holds a value while the macro runs. You create one with Dim (short for dimension) and say what kind of value it holds.

The data types you will use most
TypeHoldsExample
StringText"Asha Rao"
LongA whole number (up to about 2 billion)250000
DoubleA number with decimals3.14159
BooleanTrue or FalseTrue
DateA date or time#14-Mar-2026#
VariantAnything (flexible but slower and easier to misuse)(avoid unless needed)

Rules and habits

  • Names start with a letter, have no spaces, and are not VBA keywords.
  • Choose meaningful names: unitPrice, not x.
  • Put Option Explicit at the top of every module: VBA then complains about any variable you forgot to declare, which catches spelling mistakes.
  • Use = to assign a value: the variable on the left receives the value on the right.
Worked example

A typo that Option Explicit catches

You write totl = quantity * unitPrice by mistake, meaning total.

  1. Without Option Explicit, VBA quietly makes a new variable called totl and your total stays empty.
  2. With Option Explicit, VBA stops and says Variable not defined, pointing at the typo.

Answer. Option Explicit turns silent mistakes into visible ones.

Watch out

A Long holds whole numbers only. Assigning 4.7 to a Long rounds it to 5. Use Double for decimals.

Check what you just learned

1. Which type suits a price of 45.50?
  • String
  • Long
  • Boolean
  • Double (correct)

A number with decimals suits Double.

2. Why use Option Explicit?
  • It forces you to declare variables and catches typos (correct)
  • It speeds up Excel
  • It hides errors
  • It is optional decoration

Undeclared names become errors instead of silent mistakes.
keyPoints: Dim creates a variable and its type.
Use the right type: String, Long, Double, Boolean, Date.
Always use Option Explicit and meaningful names.

topics.title: Operators, MsgBox and InputBox
topics.html:
A macro becomes useful when it takes input and gives output. InputBox asks the user for something; MsgBox tells them something.

Operators
OperatorDoesExampleResult
+ - * /Arithmetic10 / 42.5
\Whole-number division10 \ 42
ModThe remainder10 Mod 42
^Power2 ^ 38
&Joins text"a" & "b"ab
= <> < > <= >=Compare5 <> 3True

Good habits with dialogs

  • InputBox always returns text: convert it with CLng, CDbl or CDate before calculating.
  • Check for Cancel: it returns an empty string.
  • Join text and numbers with &, not +.
  • Use Debug.Print while building: it writes to the Immediate window without bothering the user.

Common mistakes

  • Adding two InputBox results with +: they are text, so "2" + "3" gives "23", not 5. Convert first.
  • Forgetting that division by zero stops the macro with an error.
  • Using a MsgBox for dozens of messages: use Debug.Print while testing.
Try it yourself: What does MsgBox "Total: " & 2 + 3 show?

Model answer. Total: 5. The arithmetic is worked out before the join, so 2 + 3 becomes 5 and then the text is joined.

Check what you just learned

1. What type of value does InputBox return?
  • A number
  • Text (correct)
  • A date
  • A range

It always returns a String.

2. Which joins text?
  • +
  • *
  • & (correct)
  • ^

The ampersand joins text.

Key terms: flip and sort

Variable
A named box for a value
Dim
Declares a variable and its type
String
Text
Long
A whole number
Option Explicit
Forces variables to be declared
Comment
A note starting with an apostrophe
keyPoints: InputBox returns text; convert it before calculating.
Join with &; add with +.
Check for Cancel and use Debug.Print while testing.

modules.title: Talking to Excel: objects, ranges and sheets
modules.summary: Use the Excel object model: workbooks, worksheets and ranges, their properties and methods, and the patterns for finding data and writing results.
modules.outcome: You can read and write cells, format ranges and find the last row of data, which is the base of nearly every useful macro.
modules.intro: To make Excel do things, VBA talks to Excel's objects: the workbook, the sheets in it, the ranges on a sheet. Each object has properties (things it has, like a value or a colour) and methods (things it can do, like Copy or Clear). Once you see Excel as a set of objects arranged in a hierarchy, you can name anything in it.

topics.title: The object model: workbooks, sheets and ranges
topics.html:
Objects sit inside each other like folders. To point at a cell you name the path from the outside in, separated by dots.

Naming objects
ObjectHow you refer to itExample
ApplicationApplicationApplication.ScreenUpdating
WorkbookThisWorkbook, ActiveWorkbook, Workbooks("Name.xlsx")ThisWorkbook.Name
WorksheetWorksheets("Sales"), ActiveSheetWorksheets("Sales").Name
RangeRange("A1:B5"), Cells(row, column)Range("A1").Value
Tip

If you do not name the workbook or sheet, VBA uses the active ones. That is convenient but can hit the wrong sheet if the user clicks elsewhere: name the sheet in macros you share.

Watch out

ThisWorkbook is the file that contains the running code; ActiveWorkbook is whichever file is in front. They are the same only if you have not switched windows.

Check what you just learned

1. Which object is a single sheet tab?
  • Application
  • Workbook
  • Range
  • Worksheet (correct)

A worksheet is one sheet in a workbook.

2. What does ThisWorkbook mean?
  • The file that contains the running code (correct)
  • The file in front
  • The newest file
  • Any file

It is the workbook holding the macro.
keyPoints: Objects nest: Application > Workbook > Worksheet > Range.
Use dots to walk the path from the outside in.
Name the sheet explicitly rather than relying on the active one.

topics.title: Ranges, properties and methods
topics.html:
A Range is the object you use most. It can be one cell or many. Use properties to read or change things about it, and methods to make it do something.

Everyday properties and methods
NameKindDoes
.ValuePropertyThe value in the cell
.FormulaPropertyThe formula as typed
.Font.BoldPropertyTrue makes it bold
.Interior.ColorPropertyThe fill colour
.NumberFormatPropertyThe number format, such as "0.00"
.ClearMethodRemoves everything from the cells
.CopyMethodCopies the cells
.SelectMethodSelects the cells (rarely needed)

Habits that make code faster and clearer

  • Avoid Select and Activate. Work on the range directly.
  • Use With ... End With for several actions on the same object.
  • Use Cells(row, column) when the row or column is a variable: Cells(r, 3).
  • Use .Value explicitly; it is clearer than relying on the default.
Worked example

Write and read a cell

You want to put a total in D7 and read it back.

  1. Range("D7").Value = 2180 writes 2180.
  2. x = Range("D7").Value reads it into a variable.
  3. Range("D7").Formula = "=SUM(D2:D6)" writes a live formula instead of a fixed number.

Answer. Use Formula when the result should keep updating; use Value for a fixed number.

Common mistakes

  • Selecting a range and then acting on Selection when you could act on the range directly.
  • Forgetting that Cells takes (row, column), not (column, row).
  • Writing a number into a cell with .Value when you meant a formula, so it never updates.

Check what you just learned

1. Which line writes the number 2180 into D7?
  • Range("D7").Clear
  • Range("D7").Value = 2180 (correct)
  • Range("D7").Select
  • Range("D7").Copy

Assigning to .Value writes the number into the cell.

2. In Cells(3, 2), what is 2?
  • The row
  • The sheet
  • The column (correct)
  • The value

Cells takes the row first and then the column.
keyPoints: Properties describe an object; methods make it act.
Avoid Select; use With ... End With.
Cells(row, column) is the tool for loops.

topics.title: Finding the end of the data
topics.html:
Real data grows. A macro that always works on rows 2 to 100 will miss row 101. The standard fix is to find the last row of data every time.

Other ways to find your data
ToolDoesWatch out
End(xlUp)The last filled cell in a columnUse a column that is always filled
CurrentRegionThe block of data around a cell, up to the first blank row and columnBlank rows inside the data stop it early
UsedRangeEverything Excel thinks is in useCan include formatted but empty cells
Worked example

Loop over all the data

A table of marks with a header in row 1.

  1. Find the last row with End(xlUp).
  2. Loop from row 2 to lastRow so the header is skipped.
  3. The macro now works whether there are ten rows or ten thousand.

Answer. Finding the last row makes a macro safe for any size of data.

Watch out

Choose a column that has a value in every row for End(xlUp). If column A has blanks, the macro will stop at the last filled cell of A, which may be above the real end.

Check what you just learned

1. What does Cells(Rows.Count, 1).End(xlUp).Row give?
  • The first row
  • The sheet name
  • The number of columns
  • The last row with data in column A (correct)

It jumps up from the bottom of column A to the last filled cell.

2. Why not hard-code row 100?
  • The data may grow or shrink (correct)
  • It is illegal
  • VBA forbids it
  • It is slower

A macro should adapt to the data it finds.

Key terms: flip and sort

Object
A thing in Excel such as a workbook, sheet or range
Property
Something an object has: Value, Font.Bold
Method
Something an object can do: Copy, Clear
Range
A cell or block of cells
With ... End With
A way to act on one object several times
xlUp
The direction used to find the last cell
keyPoints: Find the last row every time; do not hard-code it.
End(xlUp) from the bottom of a column is the common method.
CurrentRegion and UsedRange are alternatives with limits.

modules.title: Decisions and loops
modules.summary: Make a macro decide with If and Select Case, repeat work with For, For Each and Do loops, and use arrays to hold lists.
modules.outcome: You can write a macro that goes through every row of data, applies a rule to each and records the result.
modules.intro: Decisions and loops are what make a macro more than a recording. Decisions let it choose between actions based on the data. Loops let it repeat an action across hundreds or thousands of rows without getting tired. Together they turn a ten-minute chore into a one-second click.

topics.title: If and Select Case
topics.html:
If ... Then ... Else runs different code depending on a test. When there are many exact choices, Select Case is easier to read.

Combining tests
OperatorMeansExample
AndBoth must be trueIf a >= 40 And b >= 40 Then
OrAt least one is trueIf a > 90 Or b > 90 Then
NotReverses a testIf Not IsEmpty(Range("A1")) Then

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting End If.
  • Using > when you mean >= (the boundary case, like exactly 40, is the commonest logic error).
  • Testing text with the wrong capitals: "pass" and "Pass" are different unless you use LCase or UCase.
  • Writing ElseIf conditions in the wrong order: put the most demanding test first.
Tip

Write the rule in plain words first (75 or more is a distinction; 40 or more is a pass; otherwise fail), then translate it line by line.

Check what you just learned

1. What ends an If block?
  • End
  • End If (correct)
  • Stop
  • Close If

A block If ends with End If.

2. Which test is the commonest source of a logic error?
  • Spelling
  • Indentation
  • The boundary, such as > instead of >= (correct)
  • Comments

Values exactly on the limit are the usual trap.
keyPoints: If chooses between actions; ElseIf adds more tests; every If ends with End If.
Select Case is clearer for many exact choices.
Check the boundary values.

topics.title: For...Next and For Each
topics.html:
A For loop repeats a block a set number of times. The counter takes each value from the start to the end.

Trace a For loop

Choose where the loop ends and how big each step is, for a loop that starts at 1 and does x = x + i each time.

Adjust For i = 1 To, Step and see Times the loop runs, Final x (x = x + i) change.

Definition

For Each. A loop that visits every item in a group (a collection of worksheets or every cell in a range) without counting. For Each ws In ThisWorkbook.Worksheets visits every sheet.

Choosing

  • For...Next when you know the start and the end (rows 2 to lastRow).
  • For Each when you want every item in a group (every sheet, every cell in a selection).
  • Use Exit For to leave a loop early, for example when you have found what you want.
Watch out

A loop that goes the wrong way (For i = 5 To 1 with the default Step of 1) never runs at all. To count down, write For i = 5 To 1 Step -1.

Check what you just learned

1. How many times does For i = 1 To 5 run?
  • 4
  • 1
  • 6
  • 5 (correct)

i takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.

2. Which loop visits every worksheet?
  • For Each ws In Worksheets (correct)
  • For i = 1 To 5
  • Do Until
  • If

For Each steps through every item of a collection.
keyPoints: For...Next repeats a known number of times.
For Each visits every item in a group.
Start at the first data row, not the header.

topics.title: Do loops and arrays
topics.html:
A Do loop repeats while (or until) a condition holds. It suits jobs where you do not know in advance how many times.

Do loop forms
FormRepeatsUse for
Do While test ... LoopWhile the test is trueUntil something changes
Do Until test ... LoopUntil the test becomes trueSame idea, read the other way
Do ... Loop While testAt least once, then while trueAsk again until valid
Watch out

A Do loop that never changes its test runs forever and freezes Excel. Make sure something inside the loop (like r = r + 1) moves it towards the end. Press Ctrl+Break to stop a runaway macro.

An array is a numbered list of values held under one name. Use one when you need to keep many values in memory, for example every mark so you can find the highest.

Tip

Reading a whole range into an array with arr = Range("A2:C500").Value and looping over the array is far faster than reading cell by cell on a big sheet.

Try it yourself: Which loop would you use to keep asking a user for a number until they type a valid one?

Model answer. A Do loop, because you cannot know how many attempts it will take.

Check what you just learned

1. What stops a runaway macro?
  • Ctrl+C
  • Ctrl+Break (correct)
  • Alt+F4 only
  • Nothing can

Ctrl+Break interrupts running code.

2. When is a Do loop better than a For loop?
  • When the count is known
  • Never
  • When you repeat until a condition changes (correct)
  • Only for text

A Do loop repeats while or until something changes.
keyPoints: Do While and Do Until repeat until a condition changes.
Make sure something inside the loop moves it towards the end.
Arrays hold many values under one name.

topics.title: Patterns: process every row
topics.html:
Almost every useful macro is one of a few patterns: go through rows, do something to each, and perhaps collect a result.

Four patterns you will use again and again
PatternIdeaSketch
Fill a columnCalculate a value for every rowFor r = 2 To lastRow: Cells(r, 4) = ... : Next r
Flag rowsTest each row and mark itIf Cells(r, 3) < 40 Then Cells(r, 4) = "Fail"
TallyCount or add what matchesIf rule Then count = count + 1
Delete rowsRemove rows that matchLoop from the bottom up: For r = lastRow To 2 Step -1
Worked example

Check a macro against a formula

The tally above should match COUNTIF and SUMIF.

  1. =COUNTIF(B2:B7,">=40") gives the number of passes.
  2. =SUMIF(B2:B7,">=40") gives their total.
  3. If the macro and the formulas disagree, one of them has a mistake.

Answer. A formula is a good independent check on a macro.

Watch out

When you delete rows in a loop, work from the bottom up (Step -1). Deleting from the top shifts the rows beneath up, so the loop skips the row that moved into the gap.

Check what you just learned

1. Why delete rows from the bottom up?
  • It is faster
  • It saves memory
  • VBA requires it
  • Deleting from the top makes the loop skip rows (correct)

Rows beneath shift up and one can be skipped.

2. What is a good independent check on a tally macro?
  • A COUNTIF or SUMIF formula (correct)
  • Nothing
  • A bigger font
  • A new sheet

A formula gives the same answer another way.

Key terms: flip and sort

If ... Then
Runs code only when a test is true
Select Case
Chooses between exact options
For ... Next
Repeats a set number of times
For Each
Visits every item in a group
Do While
Repeats while a condition is true
Array
A numbered list of values under one name
keyPoints: Fill, flag, tally and delete are the four basic row patterns.
Check macro results against a formula.
Delete rows from the bottom up.

modules.title: Procedures, errors and debugging
modules.summary: Structure code with Subs that take arguments and Functions you can use in cells, handle errors gracefully, and find bugs with the debugger.
modules.outcome: You can break a big job into small procedures, write a custom worksheet function, and track down why a macro misbehaves.
modules.intro: As macros grow, one long Sub becomes hard to read and harder to fix. Professionals split work into small procedures, each doing one job with a clear name, and they plan for things going wrong. This module teaches you to structure code, handle errors, and debug methodically instead of guessing.

topics.title: Subs with arguments, and Functions
topics.html:
A Sub does something. A Function works something out and returns a value. Both can take arguments: values passed in so the same procedure can be used in many places.

Sub or Function?
Use a Sub whenUse a Function when
You perform an action (format, copy, delete)You calculate a value and give it back
You do not need a value backYou want to use it in a worksheet formula as well
Example: FormatHeaderExample: GSTAmount or GradeLetter
Worked example

A function in a cell

You write GSTAmount in a standard module.

  1. In a cell type =GSTAmount(B2,0.18).
  2. Excel calls your Function and shows the result, just like a built-in function.
  3. Change B2 and the answer updates by itself.

Answer. A user-defined function extends Excel with your own calculations.

Rules of good procedures

  • One procedure, one job, with a name that says it (CalculateTotal, not Proc1).
  • Pass in what it needs as arguments rather than reaching for global values.
  • Keep each procedure to about a screen of code.
  • Put a comment above each saying what it does and what it expects.
Watch out

A user-defined function used in a cell cannot change other cells or the sheet. It can only calculate and return a value.

Check what you just learned

1. Which can be used in a worksheet cell?
  • A Sub
  • A Function (correct)
  • A comment
  • A loop

A Function returns a value that the cell shows.

2. How does a Function return its value?
  • With Return
  • With MsgBox
  • By assigning to its own name (correct)
  • With End

Assign the result to the function's name.
keyPoints: A Sub does; a Function returns a value.
Arguments let one procedure serve many cases.
A Function can be used in a worksheet cell.

topics.title: Handling errors
topics.html:
A run-time error stops a macro in a box of yellow code. For your own use that is fine; for a macro others will use, you should plan for the errors you can expect: a missing sheet, an empty cell, text where a number should be.

Error-handling tools
ToolDoes
On Error GoTo labelOn an error, jump to the label
Err.Number and Err.DescriptionSay what went wrong
Exit SubLeaves before the handler on success
On Error Resume NextIgnore errors and carry on (dangerous)
On Error GoTo 0Turns error handling off again
Watch out

On Error Resume Next hides every error, including real mistakes, and lets the macro carry on with wrong data. Use it only around one line you expect to fail, and switch it off straight afterwards.

Prevent before you handle

  • Check first if a sheet exists, a cell is empty or a number is not zero, instead of waiting for an error.
  • Validate input from InputBox before using it.
  • Tell the user what went wrong in plain words.
  • Always put Exit Sub before the handler.
Worked example

Check, do not just catch

Dividing by a number that might be zero.

  1. Better: If b <> 0 Then Range("C1").Value = a / b Else Range("C1").Value = "n/a".
  2. A simple check is clearer than an error handler for a case you can predict.

Answer. Use error handlers for the unexpected and If for the expected.

Check what you just learned

1. Why put Exit Sub before the error handler?
  • It is optional
  • To close Excel
  • It speeds up code
  • So the macro does not run the handler when everything worked (correct)

Otherwise the code flows into the handler.

2. Which is the risk of On Error Resume Next?
  • It hides real errors (correct)
  • It is slow
  • It deletes files
  • It needs Excel 365

It lets the macro carry on with wrong data.
keyPoints: On Error GoTo jumps to a handler; Err.Description says what happened.
Put Exit Sub before the handler.
Prevent expected problems with If; handle the unexpected.

topics.title: Debugging like a professional
topics.html:
Debugging is finding out why code does what it does. The method matters more than cleverness: observe, then change one thing.

The debugger's tools
ToolKeyUse it to
Step intoF8Run one line at a time and watch what happens
BreakpointF9Stop at a chosen line when running normally
Run to cursorCtrl+F8Run until the line your cursor is on
Immediate windowCtrl+GAsk for a value: ? lastRow, or test a line
Watch windowView > WatchSee a variable change as the code runs
Debug.Print(code)Write values to the Immediate window while the macro runs
Worked example

The total is 10 too high

A tally macro always adds an extra 10.

  1. Set a breakpoint at the start of the loop and press F5.
  2. Press F8 and watch the row variable: it starts at 1, not 2, so the header (10) is included.
  3. Change For r = 1 To lastRow to For r = 2 To lastRow and test again.

Answer. Stepping through shows exactly where the code and your intention part ways.

Habits that prevent bugs

  • Use Option Explicit and meaningful names.
  • Write and test small pieces before joining them.
  • Test the edges: an empty sheet, one row, the largest realistic data.
  • Keep a copy before big changes.
Tip

Hover over a variable while the code is paused to see its current value in a small tooltip.

Check what you just learned

1. Which key runs the code one line at a time?
  • F5
  • F8 (correct)
  • F9
  • F12

F8 steps into the next line.

2. What is the best first step when a macro gives a wrong answer?
  • Rewrite it all
  • Ignore it
  • Reproduce it with a small example and step through (correct)
  • Add On Error Resume Next

Observation comes before changes.
keyPoints: Reproduce, step with F8, find the first wrong line, change one thing.
Immediate and Watch windows show values.
Test the edges: empty, one row, large data.

topics.title: Events: macros that run by themselves
topics.html:
An event is something that happens in Excel: a workbook opens, a cell changes, a sheet is activated. An event procedure is a Sub that runs automatically when it does.

Common events
EventRuns whenLives in
Workbook_OpenThe file is openedThisWorkbook
Worksheet_ChangeA cell on the sheet is changedThat sheet's code module
Worksheet_SelectionChangeThe selection movesThat sheet's code module
Workbook_BeforeSaveJust before savingThisWorkbook
Watch out

Writing to a cell inside Worksheet_Change triggers the same event again, which can loop forever. Switch events off with Application.EnableEvents = False before you write, and switch them back on straight after.

Use events sparingly

  • Keep event code short and fast; it runs every time.
  • Always switch events back on, even if an error occurs (put it in the error handler too).
  • Tell users the workbook has automatic behaviour.

Check what you just learned

1. Which event runs when a cell on a sheet changes?
  • Workbook_Open
  • Worksheet_Activate
  • Workbook_BeforeSave
  • Worksheet_Change (correct)

Worksheet_Change runs when a cell changes.

2. Why switch EnableEvents off before writing in a Change event?
  • To stop the write triggering the event again in a loop (correct)
  • To save memory
  • Excel requires it
  • To hide the code

Otherwise the event calls itself endlessly.

Key terms: flip and sort

Procedure
A Sub or a Function
Argument
A value passed into a procedure
Function
A procedure that returns a value
Error handler
Code that runs when an error occurs
Breakpoint
A line where running pauses
Event
Something that triggers a procedure automatically
keyPoints: Events run macros automatically when something happens.
Switch EnableEvents off before writing inside Change events.
Keep event code short and switch events back on.

modules.title: Automation in practice
modules.summary: Put it all together: automate reports, clean and consolidate data, make macros fast and safe, and design them so others can use and maintain them.
modules.outcome: You can plan, build, test and hand over a macro that saves real time, and judge when not to automate.
modules.intro: A macro is only valuable if people trust it and can keep it working. In this last module you meet the patterns professionals automate most, learn how to keep macros fast and safe, and practise the skill that matters most: designing before coding.

topics.title: Real tasks worth automating
topics.html:
Four jobs make up most of the macros people actually use: formatting reports, cleaning data, combining files or sheets, and producing outputs such as PDFs.

Common automation jobs
JobWhat the macro doesIdeas it uses
Format the weekly reportApplies fonts, number formats, borders, column widths and totalsRanges, With, last row
Clean a data exportTrims spaces, fixes capitals, removes blank rows, converts text numbersLoops, If, string functions
Combine sheets or filesCopies data from many sheets into oneFor Each, last row, Copy
Produce outputsSaves each sheet as a PDF or sends a fileLoops, file paths
Worked example

Plan it in plain words first

The monthly branch report: six sheets, one summary.

  1. Inputs: six branch sheets with the same columns.
  2. Output: a Summary sheet with every row and a total.
  3. Steps: clear Summary, loop over branch sheets, copy rows to the next free row, total, format.
  4. Risks: a sheet with no data; a sheet in a different layout.

Answer. A page of plain-words planning saves hours of rewriting code.

Watch out

The macro assumes every branch sheet has the same columns. If a sheet differs, the Summary will be wrong without any error. Check the layout in code, and say so if it is not what you expect.

Check what you just learned

1. Which loop would combine every sheet?
  • For r = 1 To 3
  • For Each ws In ThisWorkbook.Worksheets (correct)
  • Do Until
  • If

For Each steps through every sheet.

2. What should you do before writing code?
  • Nothing
  • Choose colours
  • Plan inputs, outputs, steps and risks in plain words (correct)
  • Delete data

Planning prevents rewriting.
keyPoints: Most macros format, clean, combine or output.
Plan inputs, outputs, steps and risks in plain words first.
Check that the data has the layout the macro assumes.

topics.title: Fast, safe and tidy macros
topics.html:
A macro that takes five minutes will not be used. A macro that damages data once will never be used again. Speed and safety come from a few habits.

Speed-ups that matter
SettingEffectRemember to
Application.ScreenUpdating = FalseStops the screen redrawing at each stepSet it back to True at the end, and in the error handler
Application.Calculation = xlCalculationManualStops recalculation until you are doneRestore xlCalculationAutomatic
Avoid Select and ActivateActs on ranges directlyUse With and variables
Read ranges into arraysFar fewer calls to the sheetWrite the results back in one go

Safety habits

  • Back up the workbook before the macro changes anything important.
  • Test on a copy and on small data first.
  • Ask before destroying: a MsgBox with Yes and No before deleting.
  • Log what the macro did (a message or a hidden sheet) so a result can be checked.
  • Never hard-code file paths that only exist on your computer.
Watch out

If a macro turns ScreenUpdating off and then crashes, Excel can look frozen. Always put the settings back in a handler that runs whatever happens.

Tip

To make a macro easy to maintain, keep settings (sheet names, column numbers, a tax rate) as constants at the top of the module, not buried in the code.

Check what you just learned

1. Why restore ScreenUpdating at the end?
  • It is optional
  • To delete data
  • It speeds up code
  • Otherwise Excel looks frozen (correct)

Leaving it off leaves the screen not redrawing.

2. Which habit prevents loss if a macro goes wrong?
  • Backing up before running (correct)
  • Skipping tests
  • Hard-coding paths
  • Using On Error Resume Next

A backup lets you start again.
keyPoints: Turn off screen updating and automatic calculation, and always turn them back on.
Back up, test on a copy, ask before destroying.
Keep settings as constants at the top.

topics.title: Hand it over: documentation, sharing and when not to automate
topics.html:
A macro you cannot explain, others cannot maintain. A few small things make the difference between a clever trick and a tool the team depends on.

A hand-over checklist

  1. A short description at the top of each procedure: what it does, what it needs, what it changes.
  2. A Read me sheet in the workbook: purpose, how to run it, who to ask.
  3. A button on the sheet to run it, labelled clearly.
  4. Error messages that say what to do next.
  5. A version number and date in a comment, with a list of changes.
  6. The file saved as .xlsm, with an unprotected master copy kept safe.
When not to automate
SituationWhy
The process is still changing every weekYou will rewrite the macro each time
A formula, filter or PivotTable already does itSimple tools are easier to maintain than code
It needs judgementA rule cannot replace a person
Nobody will maintain the macroA macro nobody understands becomes a risk
Worked example

Formula first

You need totals by region.

  1. A SUMIFS or a PivotTable already does it, with no code.
  2. A macro would add something to maintain and could break.
  3. Automate only when the simpler tools cannot do the job.

Answer. The best code is often the code you did not need to write.

Watch out

Security: share macro workbooks only with people who expect them, explain why macros are needed, and never ask people to lower their macro security.

Check what you just learned

1. What belongs on a Read me sheet?
  • Passwords
  • Purpose, how to run it and who to ask (correct)
  • Nothing
  • Random notes

A new user needs to know what it is and how to use it.

2. When should you not write a macro?
  • When it is slow
  • When it is repeated
  • When a formula or PivotTable already does the job (correct)
  • When it is useful

Simple tools are easier to keep working.

Key terms: flip and sort

ScreenUpdating
Whether Excel redraws the screen while running
Constant
A named value that never changes
Read me sheet
A sheet that explains the workbook
Hand-over
Passing a macro to others with documentation
Consolidate
Combine data from many sheets into one
Maintainable
Easy for someone else to understand and fix
keyPoints: Document each procedure and add a Read me sheet.
Show errors that say what to do next.
Prefer simple tools first; automate when they cannot do the job.
